Standards Track                    [Page 22]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":2781,"children":2782},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":2784,"children":2785},{"class":545},[2786,2790,2791,2799,2801,2805,2807,2811,2812,2816,2818,2827,2829,2833,2835],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":2787,"children":2789},{"id":2788},"page-23",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":2792,"children":2793},{"class":532},[2794,2798],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2795,"children":2796},{"href":557},[2797],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":2800},"\n\n\n      segment       = *pchar\n      segment-nz    = 1*pchar\n      segment-nz-nc = 1*( unreserved \u002F pct-encoded \u002F sub-delims \u002F \"@\" )\n                    ; non-zero-length segment without any colon \":\"\n\n      pchar         = unreserved \u002F pct-encoded \u002F sub-delims \u002F \":\" \u002F \"@\"\n\n   A path consists of a sequence of path segments separated by a slash\n   (\"\u002F\") character.  A path is always defined for a URI, though the\n   defined path may be empty (zero length).  Use of the slash character\n   to indicate hierarchy is only required when a URI will be used as the\n   context for relative references.  For example, the URI\n   \u003Cmailto:fred@example.com> has a path of \"fred@example.com\", whereas\n   the URI \u003Cfoo:\u002F\u002Finfo.example.com?fred> has an empty path.\n\n   The path segments \".\" and \"..\", also known as dot-segments, are\n   defined for relative reference within the path name hierarchy.  They\n   are intended for use at the beginning of a relative-path reference\n   (",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2802,"children":2803},{"href":954},[2804],{"type":488,"textContent":2093},{"type":488,"textContent":2806},") to indicate relative position within the hierarchical\n   tree of names.  This is similar to their role within some operating\n   systems' file directory structures to indicate the current directory\n   and parent directory, respectively.  However, unlike in a file\n   system, these dot-segments are only interpreted within the URI path\n   hierarchy and are removed as part of the resolution process (",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2808,"children":2809},{"href":1094},[2810],{"type":488,"textContent":2313},{"type":488,"textContent":711},{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2813,"children":2814},{"href":1094},[2815],{"type":488,"textContent":1097},{"type":488,"textContent":2817},").\n\n   Aside from dot-segments in hierarchical paths, a path segment is\n   considered opaque by the generic syntax.  URI producing applications\n   often use the reserved characters allowed in a segment to delimit\n   scheme-specific or dereference-handler-specific subcomponents.  For\n   example, the semicolon (\";\") and equals (\"=\") reserved characters are\n   often used to delimit parameters and parameter values applicable to\n   that segment.  The comma (\",\") reserved character is often used for\n   similar purposes.  For example, one URI producer might use a segment\n   such as \"name;v=1.1\" to indicate a reference to version 1.1 of\n   \"name\", whereas another might use a segment such as \"name,1.1\" to\n   indicate the same.  Parameter types may be defined by scheme-specific\n   semantics, but in most cases the syntax of a parameter is specific to\n   the implementation of the URI's dereferencing algorithm.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":2819,"children":2820},{"class":1777},[2821,2825],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2822,"children":2823},{"class":1660,"id":217,"href":897},[2824],{"type":488,"textContent":900},{"type":488,"textContent":2826},".  Query",{"type":488,"textContent":2828},"\n\n   The query component contains non-hierarchical data that, along with\n   data in the path component (",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2830,"children":2831},{"href":884},[2832],{"type":488,"textContent":2134},{"type":488,"textContent":2834},"), serves to identify a\n   resource within the scope of the URI's scheme and naming authority\n   (if any).  The query component is indicated by the first question\n   mark (\"?\") character and terminated by a number sign (\"#\") character\n   or by the end of the URI.\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":2836,"children":2837},{"class":532},[2838],{"type":488,"textContent":2839},"Berners-Lee, et al.         Standards Track                    [Page 23]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":2842,"children":2843},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":2845,"children":2846},{"class":545},[2847,2851,2852,2860,2862,2867,2869,2878,2880,2886,2888],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":2848,"children":2850},{"id":2849},"page-24",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":2853,"children":2854},{"class":532},[2855,2859],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2856,"children":2857},{"href":557},[2858],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":2861},"\n\n\n      query       = *( pchar \u002F \"\u002F\" \u002F \"?\" )\n\n   The characters slash (\"\u002F\") and question mark (\"?\") may represent data\n   within the query component.  Beware that some older, erroneous\n   implementations may not handle such data correctly when it is used as\n   the base URI for relative references (",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2863,"children":2864},{"href":1025},[2865],{"type":488,"textContent":2866},"Section 5.1",{"type":488,"textContent":2868},"), apparently\n   because they fail to distinguish query data from path data when\n   looking for hierarchical separators.  However, as query components\n   are often used to carry identifying information in the form of\n   \"key=value\" pairs and one frequently used value is a reference to\n   another URI, it is sometimes better for usability to avoid percent-\n   encoding those characters.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":2870,"children":2871},{"class":1777},[2872,2876],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2873,"children":2874},{"class":1660,"id":222,"href":912},[2875],{"type":488,"textContent":915},{"type":488,"textContent":2877},".  Fragment",{"type":488,"textContent":2879},"\n\n   The fragment identifier component of a URI allows indirect\n   identification of a secondary resource by reference to a primary\n   resource and additional identifying information.  The identified\n   secondary resource may be some portion or subset of the primary\n   resource, some view on representations of the primary resource, or\n   some other resource defined or described by those representations.  A\n   fragment identifier component is indicated by the presence of a\n   number sign (\"#\") character and terminated by the end of the URI.\n\n      fragment    = *( pchar \u002F \"\u002F\" \u002F \"?\" )\n\n   The semantics of a fragment identifier are defined by the set of\n   representations that might result from a retrieval action on the\n   primary resource.  The fragment's format and resolution is therefore\n   dependent on the media type [",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2881,"children":2883},{"href":2882},"\u002Finfo\u002Frfc2046\u002F",[2884],{"type":488,"textContent":2885},"RFC2046",{"type":488,"textContent":2887},"] of a potentially retrieved\n   representation, even though such a retrieval is only performed if the\n   URI is dereferenced.  If no such representation exists, then the\n   semantics of the fragment are considered unknown and are effectively\n   unconstrained.  Fragment identifier semantics are independent of the\n   URI scheme and thus cannot be redefined by scheme specifications.\n\n   Individual media types may define their own restrictions on or\n   structures within the fragment identifier syntax for specifying\n   different types of subsets, views, or external references that are\n   identifiable as secondary resources by that media type.  If the\n   primary resource has multiple representations, as is often the case\n   for resources whose representation is selected based on attributes of\n   the retrieval request (a.k.a., content negotiation), then whatever is\n   identified by the fragment should be consistent across all of those\n   representations.  Each representation should either define the\n   fragment so that it corresponds to the same secondary resource,\n   regardless of how it is represented, or should leave the fragment\n   undefined (i.e., not found).\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":2889,"children":2890},{"class":532},[2891],{"type":488,"textContent":2892},"Berners-Lee, et al.         Standards Track                    [Page 24]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":2895,"children":2896},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":2898,"children":2899},{"class":545},[2900,2904,2905,2913,2915,2919,2920,2924,2925,2934,2936,2945,2947],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":2901,"children":2903},{"id":2902},"page-25",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":2906,"children":2907},{"class":532},[2908,2912],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2909,"children":2910},{"href":557},[2911],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":2914},"\n\n\n   As with any URI, use of a fragment identifier component does not\n   imply that a retrieval action will take place.  A URI with a fragment\n   identifier may be used to refer to the secondary resource without any\n   implication that the primary resource is accessible or will ever be\n   accessed.\n\n   Fragment identifiers have a special role in information retrieval\n   systems as the primary form of client-side indirect referencing,\n   allowing an author to specifically identify aspects of an existing\n   resource that are only indirectly provided by the resource owner.  As\n   such, the fragment identifier is not used in the scheme-specific\n   processing of a URI; instead, the fragment identifier is separated\n   from the rest of the URI prior to a dereference, and thus the\n   identifying information within the fragment itself is dereferenced\n   solely by the user agent, regardless of the URI scheme.  Although\n   this separate handling is often perceived to be a loss of\n   information, particularly for accurate redirection of references as\n   resources move over time, it also serves to prevent information\n   providers from denying reference authors the right to refer to\n   information within a resource selectively.  Indirect referencing also\n   provides additional flexibility and extensibility to systems that use\n   URIs, as new media types are easier to define and deploy than new\n   schemes of identification.\n\n   The characters slash (\"\u002F\") and question mark (\"?\") are allowed to\n   represent data within the fragment identifier.  Beware that some\n   older, erroneous implementations may not handle this data correctly\n   when it is used as the base URI for relative references (",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2916,"children":2917},{"href":1025},[2918],{"type":488,"textContent":2313},{"type":488,"textContent":711},{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2921,"children":2922},{"href":1025},[2923],{"type":488,"textContent":1028},{"type":488,"textContent":2498},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":2926,"children":2927},{"class":1656},[2928,2932],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2929,"children":2930},{"class":1660,"id":227,"href":927},[2931],{"type":488,"textContent":578},{"type":488,"textContent":2933},".  Usage",{"type":488,"textContent":2935},"\n\n   When applications make reference to a URI, they do not always use the\n   full form of reference defined by the \"URI\" syntax rule.  To save\n   space and take advantage of hierarchical locality, many Internet\n   protocol elements and media type formats allow an abbreviation of a\n   URI, whereas others restrict the syntax to a particular form of URI.\n   We define the most common forms of reference syntax in this\n   specification because they impact and depend upon the design of the\n   generic syntax, requiring a uniform parsing algorithm in order to be\n   interpreted consistently.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":2937,"children":2938},{"class":1777},[2939,2943],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2940,"children":2941},{"class":1660,"id":233,"href":941},[2942],{"type":488,"textContent":944},{"type":488,"textContent":2944},".  URI Reference",{"type":488,"textContent":2946},"\n\n   URI-reference is used to denote the most common usage of a resource\n   identifier.\n\n      URI-reference = URI \u002F relative-ref\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":2948,"children":2949},{"class":532},[2950],{"type":488,"textContent":2951},"Berners-Lee, et al.         Standards Track                    [Page 25]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":2954,"children":2955},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":2957,"children":2958},{"class":545},[2959,2963,2964,2972,2974,2979,2981,2990,2992,2997,2999,3003,3005],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":2960,"children":2962},{"id":2961},"page-26",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":2965,"children":2966},{"class":532},[2967,2971],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2968,"children":2969},{"href":557},[2970],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":2973},"\n\n\n   A URI-reference is either a URI or a relative reference.  If the\n   URI-reference's prefix does not match the syntax of a scheme followed\n   by its colon separator, then the URI-reference is a relative\n   reference.\n\n   A URI-reference is typically parsed first into the five URI\n   components, in order to determine what components are present and\n   whether the reference is relative.  Then, each component is parsed\n   for its subparts and their validation.  The ABNF of URI-reference,\n   along with the \"first-match-wins\" disambiguation rule, is sufficient\n   to define a validating parser for the generic syntax.  Readers\n   familiar with regular expressions should see ",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2975,"children":2976},{"href":1526},[2977],{"type":488,"textContent":2978},"Appendix B",{"type":488,"textContent":2980}," for an\n   example of a non-validating URI-reference parser that will take any\n   given string and extract the URI components.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":2982,"children":2983},{"class":1777},[2984,2988],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2985,"children":2986},{"class":1660,"id":238,"href":954},[2987],{"type":488,"textContent":957},{"type":488,"textContent":2989},".  Relative Reference",{"type":488,"textContent":2991},"\n\n   A relative reference takes advantage of the hierarchical syntax\n   (",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":2993,"children":2994},{"href":683},[2995],{"type":488,"textContent":2996},"Section 1.2.3",{"type":488,"textContent":2998},") to express a URI reference relative to the name space\n   of another hierarchical URI.\n\n      relative-ref  = relative-part [ \"?\" query ] [ \"#\" fragment ]\n\n      relative-part = \"\u002F\u002F\" authority path-abempty\n                    \u002F path-absolute\n                    \u002F path-noscheme\n                    \u002F path-empty\n\n   The URI referred to by a relative reference, also known as the target\n   URI, is obtained by applying the reference resolution algorithm of\n   ",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3000,"children":3001},{"href":1010},[3002],{"type":488,"textContent":2127},{"type":488,"textContent":3004},".\n\n   A relative reference that begins with two slash characters is termed\n   a network-path reference; such references are rarely used.  A\n   relative reference that begins with a single slash character is\n   termed an absolute-path reference.  A relative reference that does\n   not begin with a slash character is termed a relative-path reference.\n\n   A path segment that contains a colon character (e.g., \"this:that\")\n   cannot be used as the first segment of a relative-path reference, as\n   it would be mistaken for a scheme name.  Such a segment must be\n   preceded by a dot-segment (e.g., \".\u002Fthis:that\") to make a relative-\n   path reference.\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3006,"children":3007},{"class":532},[3008],{"type":488,"textContent":3009},"Berners-Lee, et al.         Standards Track                    [Page 26]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":3012,"children":3013},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":3015,"children":3016},{"class":545},[3017,3021,3022,3030,3031,3040,3042,3051,3053,3057,3059,3063,3064,3068,3070,3079,3081],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3018,"children":3020},{"id":3019},"page-27",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3023,"children":3024},{"class":532},[3025,3029],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3026,"children":3027},{"href":557},[3028],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":1653},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3032,"children":3033},{"class":1777},[3034,3038],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3035,"children":3036},{"class":1660,"id":243,"href":969},[3037],{"type":488,"textContent":972},{"type":488,"textContent":3039},".  Absolute URI",{"type":488,"textContent":3041},"\n\n   Some protocol elements allow only the absolute form of a URI without\n   a fragment identifier.  For example, defining a base URI for later\n   use by relative references calls for an absolute-URI syntax rule that\n   does not allow a fragment.\n\n      absolute-URI  = scheme \":\" hier-part [ \"?\" query ]\n\n   URI scheme specifications must define their own syntax so that all\n   strings matching their scheme-specific syntax will also match the\n   \u003Cabsolute-URI> grammar.  Scheme specifications will not define\n   fragment identifier syntax or usage, regardless of its applicability\n   to resources identifiable via that scheme, as fragment identification\n   is orthogonal to scheme definition.  However, scheme specifications\n   are encouraged to include a wide range of examples, including\n   examples that show use of the scheme's URIs with fragment identifiers\n   when such usage is appropriate.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3043,"children":3044},{"class":1777},[3045,3049],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3046,"children":3047},{"class":1660,"id":248,"href":984},[3048],{"type":488,"textContent":987},{"type":488,"textContent":3050},".  Same-Document Reference",{"type":488,"textContent":3052},"\n\n   When a URI reference refers to a URI that is, aside from its fragment\n   component (if any), identical to the base URI (",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3054,"children":3055},{"href":1025},[3056],{"type":488,"textContent":2866},{"type":488,"textContent":3058},"), that\n   reference is called a \"same-document\" reference.  The most frequent\n   examples of same-document references are relative references that are\n   empty or include only the number sign (\"#\") separator followed by a\n   fragment identifier.\n\n   When a same-document reference is dereferenced for a retrieval\n   action, the target of that reference is defined to be within the same\n   entity (representation, document, or message) as the reference;\n   therefore, a dereference should not result in a new retrieval action.\n\n   Normalization of the base and target URIs prior to their comparison,\n   as described in Sections ",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3060,"children":3061},{"href":1304},[3062],{"type":488,"textContent":1307},{"type":488,"textContent":2689},{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3065,"children":3066},{"href":1319},[3067],{"type":488,"textContent":1322},{"type":488,"textContent":3069},", is allowed but rarely\n   performed in practice.  Normalization may increase the set of same-\n   document references, which may be of benefit to some caching\n   applications.  As such, reference authors should not assume that a\n   slightly different, though equivalent, reference URI will (or will\n   not) be interpreted as a same-document reference by any given\n   application.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3071,"children":3072},{"class":1777},[3073,3077],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3074,"children":3075},{"class":1660,"id":253,"href":997},[3076],{"type":488,"textContent":1000},{"type":488,"textContent":3078},".  Suffix Reference",{"type":488,"textContent":3080},"\n\n   The URI syntax is designed for unambiguous reference to resources and\n   extensibility via the URI scheme.  However, as URI identification and\n   usage have become commonplace, traditional media (television, radio,\n   newspapers, billboards, etc.) have increasingly used a suffix of the\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3082,"children":3083},{"class":532},[3084],{"type":488,"textContent":3085},"Berners-Lee, et al.         Standards Track                    [Page 27]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":3088,"children":3089},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":3091,"children":3092},{"class":545},[3093,3097,3098,3106,3108,3114,3116,3125,3127,3131,3132,3141,3143,3148,3150,3154,3156],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3094,"children":3096},{"id":3095},"page-28",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3099,"children":3100},{"class":532},[3101,3105],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3102,"children":3103},{"href":557},[3104],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":3107},"\n\n\n   URI as a reference, consisting of only the authority and path\n   portions of the URI, such as\n\n      www.w3.org\u002FAddressing\u002F\n\n   or simply a DNS registered name on its own.  Such references are\n   primarily intended for human interpretation rather than for machines,\n   with the assumption that context-based heuristics are sufficient to\n   complete the URI (e.g., most registered names beginning with \"www\"\n   are likely to have a URI prefix of \"http:\u002F\u002F\").  Although there is no\n   standard set of heuristics for disambiguating a URI suffix, many\n   client implementations allow them to be entered by the user and\n   heuristically resolved.\n\n   Although this practice of using suffix references is common, it\n   should be avoided whenever possible and should never be used in\n   situations where long-term references are expected.  The heuristics\n   noted above will change over time, particularly when a new URI scheme\n   becomes popular, and are often incorrect when used out of context.\n   Furthermore, they can lead to security issues along the lines of\n   those described in [",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3109,"children":3111},{"href":3110},"\u002Finfo\u002Frfc1535\u002F",[3112],{"type":488,"textContent":3113},"RFC1535",{"type":488,"textContent":3115},"].\n\n   As a URI suffix has the same syntax as a relative-path reference, a\n   suffix reference cannot be used in contexts where a relative\n   reference is expected.  As a result, suffix references are limited to\n   places where there is no defined base URI, such as dialog boxes and\n   off-line advertisements.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3117,"children":3118},{"class":1656},[3119,3123],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3120,"children":3121},{"class":1660,"id":258,"href":1010},[3122],{"type":488,"textContent":1013},{"type":488,"textContent":3124},".  Reference Resolution",{"type":488,"textContent":3126},"\n\n   This section defines the process of resolving a URI reference within\n   a context that allows relative references so that the result is a\n   string matching the \u003CURI> syntax rule of ",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3128,"children":3129},{"href":798},[3130],{"type":488,"textContent":1818},{"type":488,"textContent":2162},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3133,"children":3134},{"class":1777},[3135,3139],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3136,"children":3137},{"class":1660,"id":264,"href":1025},[3138],{"type":488,"textContent":1028},{"type":488,"textContent":3140},".  Establishing a Base URI",{"type":488,"textContent":3142},"\n\n   The term \"relative\" implies that a \"base URI\" exists against which\n   the relative reference is applied.  Aside from fragment-only\n   references (",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3144,"children":3145},{"href":984},[3146],{"type":488,"textContent":3147},"Section 4.4",{"type":488,"textContent":3149},"), relative references are only usable when a\n   base URI is known.  A base URI must be established by the parser\n   prior to parsing URI references that might be relative.  A base URI\n   must conform to the \u003Cabsolute-URI> syntax rule (",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3151,"children":3152},{"href":969},[3153],{"type":488,"textContent":2489},{"type":488,"textContent":3155},").  If the\n   base URI is obtained from a URI reference, then that reference must\n   be converted to absolute form and stripped of any fragment component\n   prior to its use as a base URI.\n\n\n\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3157,"children":3158},{"class":532},[3159],{"type":488,"textContent":3160},"Berners-Lee, et al.         Standards Track                    [Page 28]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":3163,"children":3164},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":3166,"children":3167},{"class":545},[3168,3172,3173,3181,3183,3192,3194,3203,3205],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3169,"children":3171},{"id":3170},"page-29",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3174,"children":3175},{"class":532},[3176,3180],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3177,"children":3178},{"href":557},[3179],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":3182},"\n\n\n   The base URI of a reference can be established in one of four ways,\n   discussed below in order of precedence.  The order of precedence can\n   be thought of in terms of layers, where the innermost defined base\n   URI has the highest precedence.  This can be visualized graphically\n   as follows:\n\n         .----------------------------------------------------------.\n         |  .----------------------------------------------------.  |\n         |  |  .----------------------------------------------.  |  |\n         |  |  |  .----------------------------------------.  |  |  |\n         |  |  |  |  .----------------------------------.  |  |  |  |\n         |  |  |  |  |       \u003Crelative-reference>       |  |  |  |  |\n         |  |  |  |  `----------------------------------'  |  |  |  |\n         |  |  |  | (5.1.1) Base URI embedded in content   |  |  |  |\n         |  |  |  `----------------------------------------'  |  |  |\n         |  |  | (5.1.2) Base URI of the encapsulating entity |  |  |\n         |  |  |         (message, representation, or none)   |  |  |\n         |  |  `----------------------------------------------'  |  |\n         |  | (5.1.3) URI used to retrieve the entity            |  |\n         |  `----------------------------------------------------'  |\n         | (5.1.4) Default Base URI (application-dependent)         |\n         `----------------------------------------------------------'\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3184,"children":3185},{"class":1864},[3186,3190],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3187,"children":3188},{"class":1660,"id":270,"href":1038},[3189],{"type":488,"textContent":1041},{"type":488,"textContent":3191},".  Base URI Embedded in Content",{"type":488,"textContent":3193},"\n\n   Within certain media types, a base URI for relative references can be\n   embedded within the content itself so that it can be readily obtained\n   by a parser.  This can be useful for descriptive documents, such as\n   tables of contents, which may be transmitted to others through\n   protocols other than their usual retrieval context (e.g., email or\n   USENET news).\n\n   It is beyond the scope of this specification to specify how, for each\n   media type, a base URI can be embedded.  The appropriate syntax, when\n   available, is described by the data format specification associated\n   with each media type.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3195,"children":3196},{"class":1864},[3197,3201],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3198,"children":3199},{"class":1660,"id":275,"href":1053},[3200],{"type":488,"textContent":1056},{"type":488,"textContent":3202},".  Base URI from the Encapsulating Entity",{"type":488,"textContent":3204},"\n\n   If no base URI is embedded, the base URI is defined by the\n   representation's retrieval context.  For a document that is enclosed\n   within another entity, such as a message or archive, the retrieval\n   context is that entity.  Thus, the default base URI of a\n   representation is the base URI of the entity in which the\n   representation is encapsulated.\n\n\n\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3206,"children":3207},{"class":532},[3208],{"type":488,"textContent":3209},"Berners-Lee, et al.         Standards Track                    [Page 29]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":3212,"children":3213},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":3215,"children":3216},{"class":545},[3217,3221,3222,3230,3232,3238,3240,3249,3251,3260,3262,3271,3273,3278,3280],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3218,"children":3220},{"id":3219},"page-30",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3223,"children":3224},{"class":532},[3225,3229],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3226,"children":3227},{"href":557},[3228],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":3231},"\n\n\n   A mechanism for embedding a base URI within MIME container types\n   (e.g., the message and multipart types) is defined by MHTML\n   [",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3233,"children":3235},{"href":3234},"\u002Finfo\u002Frfc2557\u002F",[3236],{"type":488,"textContent":3237},"RFC2557",{"type":488,"textContent":3239},"].  Protocols that do not use the MIME message header syntax,\n   but that do allow some form of tagged metadata to be included within\n   messages, may define their own syntax for defining a base URI as part\n   of a message.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3241,"children":3242},{"class":1864},[3243,3247],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3244,"children":3245},{"class":1660,"id":280,"href":1066},[3246],{"type":488,"textContent":1069},{"type":488,"textContent":3248},".  Base URI from the Retrieval URI",{"type":488,"textContent":3250},"\n\n   If no base URI is embedded and the representation is not encapsulated\n   within some other entity, then, if a URI was used to retrieve the\n   representation, that URI shall be considered the base URI.  Note that\n   if the retrieval was the result of a redirected request, the last URI\n   used (i.e., the URI that resulted in the actual retrieval of the\n   representation) is the base URI.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3252,"children":3253},{"class":1864},[3254,3258],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3255,"children":3256},{"class":1660,"id":285,"href":1081},[3257],{"type":488,"textContent":1084},{"type":488,"textContent":3259},".  Default Base URI",{"type":488,"textContent":3261},"\n\n   If none of the conditions described above apply, then the base URI is\n   defined by the context of the application.  As this definition is\n   necessarily application-dependent, failing to define a base URI by\n   using one of the other methods may result in the same content being\n   interpreted differently by different types of applications.\n\n   A sender of a representation containing relative references is\n   responsible for ensuring that a base URI for those references can be\n   established.  Aside from fragment-only references, relative\n   references can only be used reliably in situations where the base URI\n   is well defined.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3263,"children":3264},{"class":1777},[3265,3269],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3266,"children":3267},{"class":1660,"id":290,"href":1094},[3268],{"type":488,"textContent":1097},{"type":488,"textContent":3270},".  Relative Resolution",{"type":488,"textContent":3272},"\n\n   This section describes an algorithm for converting a URI reference\n   that might be relative to a given base URI into the parsed components\n   of the reference's target.  The components can then be recomposed, as\n   described in ",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3274,"children":3275},{"href":1165},[3276],{"type":488,"textContent":3277},"Section 5.3",{"type":488,"textContent":3279},", to form the target URI.  This algorithm\n   provides definitive results that can be used to test the output of\n   other implementations.  Applications may implement relative reference\n   resolution by using some other algorithm, provided that the results\n   match what would be given by this one.\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3281,"children":3282},{"class":532},[3283],{"type":488,"textContent":3284},"Berners-Lee, et al.         Standards Track                    [Page 30]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":3287,"children":3288},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":3290,"children":3291},{"class":545},[3292,3296,3297,3305,3306,3315,3317,3321,3323,3327,3329,3333,3335,3344,3346],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3293,"children":3295},{"id":3294},"page-31",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3298,"children":3299},{"class":532},[3300,3304],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3301,"children":3302},{"href":557},[3303],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":1653},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3307,"children":3308},{"class":1864},[3309,3313],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3310,"children":3311},{"class":1660,"id":296,"href":1107},[3312],{"type":488,"textContent":1110},{"type":488,"textContent":3314},".  Pre-parse the Base URI",{"type":488,"textContent":3316},"\n\n   The base URI (Base) is established according to the procedure of\n   ",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3318,"children":3319},{"href":1025},[3320],{"type":488,"textContent":2866},{"type":488,"textContent":3322}," and parsed into the five main components described in\n   ",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3324,"children":3325},{"href":798},[3326],{"type":488,"textContent":1818},{"type":488,"textContent":3328},".  Note that only the scheme component is required to be\n   present in a base URI; the other components may be empty or\n   undefined.  A component is undefined if its associated delimiter does\n   not appear in the URI reference; the path component is never\n   undefined, though it may be empty.\n\n   Normalization of the base URI, as described in Sections ",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3330,"children":3331},{"href":1304},[3332],{"type":488,"textContent":1307},{"type":488,"textContent":3334}," and\n   6.2.3, is optional.  A URI reference must be transformed to its\n   target URI before it can be normalized.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3336,"children":3337},{"class":1864},[3338,3342],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3339,"children":3340},{"class":1660,"id":301,"href":1122},[3341],{"type":488,"textContent":1125},{"type":488,"textContent":3343},".  Transform References",{"type":488,"textContent":3345},"\n\n   For each URI reference (R), the following pseudocode describes an\n   algorithm for transforming R into its target URI (T):\n\n      -- The URI reference is parsed into the five URI components\n      --\n      (R.scheme, R.authority, R.path, R.query, R.fragment) = parse(R);\n\n      -- A non-strict parser may ignore a scheme in the reference\n      -- if it is identical to the base URI's scheme.\n      --\n      if ((not strict) and (R.scheme == Base.scheme)) then\n         undefine(R.scheme);\n      endif;\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3347,"children":3348},{"class":532},[3349],{"type":488,"textContent":3350},"Berners-Lee, et al.         Standards Track                    [Page 31]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":3353,"children":3354},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":3356,"children":3357},{"class":545},[3358,3362,3363,3371,3373,3382,3384],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3359,"children":3361},{"id":3360},"page-32",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3364,"children":3365},{"class":532},[3366,3370],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3367,"children":3368},{"href":557},[3369],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":3372},"\n\n\n      if defined(R.scheme) then\n         T.scheme    = R.scheme;\n         T.authority = R.authority;\n         T.path      = remove_dot_segments(R.path);\n         T.query     = R.query;\n      else\n         if defined(R.authority) then\n            T.authority = R.authority;\n            T.path      = remove_dot_segments(R.path);\n            T.query     = R.query;\n         else\n            if (R.path == \"\") then\n               T.path = Base.path;\n               if defined(R.query) then\n                  T.query = R.query;\n               else\n                  T.query = Base.query;\n               endif;\n            else\n               if (R.path starts-with \"\u002F\") then\n                  T.path = remove_dot_segments(R.path);\n               else\n                  T.path = merge(Base.path, R.path);\n                  T.path = remove_dot_segments(T.path);\n               endif;\n               T.query = R.query;\n            endif;\n            T.authority = Base.authority;\n         endif;\n         T.scheme = Base.scheme;\n      endif;\n\n      T.fragment = Merge Paths",{"type":488,"textContent":3383},"\n\n   The pseudocode above refers to a \"merge\" routine for merging a\n   relative-path reference with the path of the base URI.  This is\n   accomplished as follows:\n\n   o  If the base URI has a defined authority component and an empty\n      path, then return a string consisting of \"\u002F\" concatenated with the\n      reference's path; otherwise,\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3385,"children":3386},{"class":532},[3387],{"type":488,"textContent":3388},"Berners-Lee, et al.         Standards Track                    [Page 32]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":3391,"children":3392},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":3394,"children":3395},{"class":545},[3396,3400,3401,3409,3411,3420,3422],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3397,"children":3399},{"id":3398},"page-33",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3402,"children":3403},{"class":532},[3404,3408],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3405,"children":3406},{"href":557},[3407],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":3410},"\n\n\n   o  return a string consisting of the reference's path component\n      appended to all but the last segment of the base URI's path (i.e.,\n      excluding any characters after the right-most \"\u002F\" in the base URI\n      path, or excluding the entire base URI path if it does not contain\n      any \"\u002F\" characters).\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3412,"children":3413},{"class":1864},[3414,3418],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3415,"children":3416},{"class":1660,"id":311,"href":1150},[3417],{"type":488,"textContent":1153},{"type":488,"textContent":3419},".  Remove Dot Segments",{"type":488,"textContent":3421},"\n\n   The pseudocode also refers to a \"remove_dot_segments\" routine for\n   interpreting and removing the special \".\" and \"..\" complete path\n   segments from a referenced path.  This is done after the path is\n   extracted from a reference, whether or not the path was relative, in\n   order to remove any invalid or extraneous dot-segments prior to\n   forming the target URI.  Although there are many ways to accomplish\n   this removal process, we describe a simple method using two string\n   buffers.\n\n   1.  The input buffer is initialized with the now-appended path\n       components and the output buffer is initialized to the empty\n       string.\n\n   2.  While the input buffer is not empty, loop as follows:\n\n       A.  If the input buffer begins with a prefix of \"..\u002F\" or \".\u002F\",\n           then remove that prefix from the input buffer; otherwise,\n\n       B.  if the input buffer begins with a prefix of \"\u002F.\u002F\" or \"\u002F.\",\n           where \".\" is a complete path segment, then replace that\n           prefix with \"\u002F\" in the input buffer; otherwise,\n\n       C.  if the input buffer begins with a prefix of \"\u002F..\u002F\" or \"\u002F..\",\n           where \"..\" is a complete path segment, then replace that\n           prefix with \"\u002F\" in the input buffer and remove the last\n           segment and its preceding \"\u002F\" (if any) from the output\n           buffer; otherwise,\n\n       D.  if the input buffer consists only of \".\" or \"..\", then remove\n           that from the input buffer; otherwise,\n\n       E.  move the first path segment in the input buffer to the end of\n           the output buffer, including the initial \"\u002F\" character (if\n           any) and any subsequent characters up to, but not including,\n           the next \"\u002F\" character or the end of the input buffer.\n\n   3.  Finally, the output buffer is returned as the result of\n       remove_dot_segments.\n\n\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3423,"children":3424},{"class":532},[3425],{"type":488,"textContent":3426},"Berners-Lee, et al.         Standards Track                    [Page 33]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":3429,"children":3430},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":3432,"children":3433},{"class":545},[3434,3438,3439,3447,3449,3453,3455],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3435,"children":3437},{"id":3436},"page-34",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3440,"children":3441},{"class":532},[3442,3446],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3443,"children":3444},{"href":557},[3445],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":3448},"\n\n\n   Note that dot-segments are intended for use in URI references to\n   express an identifier relative to the hierarchy of names in the base\n   URI.  The remove_dot_segments algorithm respects that hierarchy by\n   removing extra dot-segments rather than treat them as an error or\n   leaving them to be misinterpreted by dereference implementations.\n\n   The following illustrates how the above steps are applied for two\n   examples of merged paths, showing the state of the two buffers after\n   each step.\n\n      STEP   OUTPUT BUFFER         INPUT BUFFER\n\n       1 :                         \u002Fa\u002Fb\u002Fc\u002F.\u002F..\u002F..\u002Fg\n       2E:   \u002Fa                    \u002Fb\u002Fc\u002F.\u002F..\u002F..\u002Fg\n       2E:   \u002Fa\u002Fb                  \u002Fc\u002F.\u002F..\u002F..\u002Fg\n       2E:   \u002Fa\u002Fb\u002Fc mid\u002Fcontent=5\u002F..\u002F6\n       2E:   mid                   \u002Fcontent=5\u002F..\u002F6\n       2E:   mid\u002Fcontent=5         \u002F..\u002F6\n       2C:   mid                   \u002F6\n       2E:   mid\u002F6\n\n   Some applications may find it more efficient to implement the\n   remove_dot_segments algorithm by using two segment stacks rather than\n   strings.\n\n Normalization and Comparison",{"type":488,"textContent":3837},"\n\n   One of the most common operations on URIs is simple comparison:\n   determining whether two URIs are equivalent without using the URIs to\n   access their respective resource(s).  A comparison is performed every\n   time a response cache is accessed, a browser checks its history to\n   color a link, or an XML parser processes tags within a namespace.\n   Extensive normalization prior to comparison of URIs is often used by\n   spiders and indexing engines to prune a search space or to reduce\n   duplication of request actions and response storage.\n\n   URI comparison is performed for some particular purpose.  Protocols\n   or implementations that compare URIs for different purposes will\n   often be subject to differing design trade-offs in regards to how\n   much effort should be spent in reducing aliased identifiers.  This\n   section describes various methods that may be used to compare URIs,\n   the trade-offs between them, and the types of applications that might\n   use them.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3839,"children":3840},{"class":1777},[3841,3845],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3842,"children":3843},{"class":1660,"id":343,"href":1263},[3844],{"type":488,"textContent":1266},{"type":488,"textContent":3846},".  Equivalence",{"type":488,"textContent":3848},"\n\n   Because URIs exist to identify resources, presumably they should be\n   considered equivalent when they identify the same resource.  However,\n   this definition of equivalence is not of much practical use, as there\n   is no way for an implementation to compare two resources unless it\n   has full knowledge or control of them.  For this reason,\n   determination of equivalence or difference of URIs is based on string\n   comparison, perhaps augmented by reference to additional rules\n   provided by URI scheme definitions.  We use the terms \"different\" and\n   \"equivalent\" to describe the possible outcomes of such comparisons,\n   but there are many application-dependent versions of equivalence.\n\n   Even though it is possible to determine that two URIs are equivalent,\n   URI comparison is not sufficient to determine whether two URIs\n   identify different resources.  For example, an owner of two different\n   domain names could decide to serve the same resource from both,\n   resulting in two different URIs.  Therefore, comparison methods are\n   designed to minimize false negatives while strictly avoiding false\n   positives.\n\n   In testing for equivalence, applications should not directly compare\n   relative references; the references should be converted to their\n   respective target URIs before comparison.  When URIs are compared to\n   select (or avoid) a network action, such as retrieval of a\n   representation, fragment components (if any) should be excluded from\n   the comparison.\n\n\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3850,"children":3851},{"class":532},[3852],{"type":488,"textContent":3853},"Berners-Lee, et al.         Standards Track                    [Page 38]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":3856,"children":3857},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":3859,"children":3860},{"class":545},[3861,3865,3866,3874,3875,3884,3886,3895,3897],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3862,"children":3864},{"id":3863},"page-39",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3867,"children":3868},{"class":532},[3869,3873],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3870,"children":3871},{"href":557},[3872],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":1653},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3876,"children":3877},{"class":1777},[3878,3882],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3879,"children":3880},{"class":1660,"id":348,"href":1276},[3881],{"type":488,"textContent":1279},{"type":488,"textContent":3883},".  Comparison Ladder",{"type":488,"textContent":3885},"\n\n   A variety of methods are used in practice to test URI equivalence.\n   These methods fall into a range, distinguished by the amount of\n   processing required and the degree to which the probability of false\n   negatives is reduced.  As noted above, false negatives cannot be\n   eliminated.  In practice, their probability can be reduced, but this\n   reduction requires more processing and is not cost-effective for all\n   applications.\n\n   If this range of comparison practices is considered as a ladder, the\n   following discussion will climb the ladder, starting with practices\n   that are cheap but have a relatively higher chance of producing false\n   negatives, and proceeding to those that have higher computational\n   cost and lower risk of false negatives.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3887,"children":3888},{"class":1864},[3889,3893],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3890,"children":3891},{"class":1660,"id":354,"href":1291},[3892],{"type":488,"textContent":1294},{"type":488,"textContent":3894},".  Simple String Comparison",{"type":488,"textContent":3896},"\n\n   If two URIs, when considered as character strings, are identical,\n   then it is safe to conclude that they are equivalent.  This type of\n   equivalence test has very low computational cost and is in wide use\n   in a variety of applications, particularly in the domain of parsing.\n\n   Testing strings for equivalence requires some basic precautions.\n   This procedure is often referred to as \"bit-for-bit\" or\n   \"byte-for-byte\" comparison, which is potentially misleading.  Testing\n   strings for equality is normally based on pair comparison of the\n   characters that make up the strings, starting from the first and\n   proceeding until both strings are exhausted and all characters are\n   found to be equal, until a pair of characters compares unequal, or\n   until one of the strings is exhausted before the other.\n\n   This character comparison requires that each pair of characters be\n   put in comparable form.  For example, should one URI be stored in a\n   byte array in EBCDIC encoding and the second in a Java String object\n   (UTF-16), bit-for-bit comparisons applied naively will produce\n   errors.  It is better to speak of equality on a character-for-\n   character basis rather than on a byte-for-byte or bit-for-bit basis.\n   In practical terms, character-by-character comparisons should be done\n   codepoint-by-codepoint after conversion to a common character\n   encoding.\n\n   False negatives are caused by the production and use of URI aliases.\n   Unnecessary aliases can be reduced, regardless of the comparison\n   method, by consistently providing URI references in an already-\n   normalized form (i.e., a form identical to what would be produced\n   after normalization is applied, as described below).\n\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3898,"children":3899},{"class":532},[3900],{"type":488,"textContent":3901},"Berners-Lee, et al.         Standards Track                    [Page 39]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":3904,"children":3905},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":3907,"children":3908},{"class":545},[3909,3913,3914,3922,3924,3933,3935,3947,3949,3954,3955,3966,3968,3972,3974,3979,3981],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3910,"children":3912},{"id":3911},"page-40",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3915,"children":3916},{"class":532},[3917,3921],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3918,"children":3919},{"href":557},[3920],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":3923},"\n\n\n   Protocols and data formats often limit some URI comparisons to simple\n   string comparison, based on the theory that people and\n   implementations will, in their own best interest, be consistent in\n   providing URI references, or at least consistent enough to negate any\n   efficiency that might be obtained from further normalization.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3925,"children":3926},{"class":1864},[3927,3931],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3928,"children":3929},{"class":1660,"id":359,"href":1304},[3930],{"type":488,"textContent":1307},{"type":488,"textContent":3932},".  Syntax-Based Normalization",{"type":488,"textContent":3934},"\n\n   Implementations may use logic based on the definitions provided by\n   this specification to reduce the probability of false negatives.\n   This processing is moderately higher in cost than character-for-\n   character string comparison.  For example, an application using this\n   approach could reasonably consider the following two URIs equivalent:\n\n      example:\u002F\u002Fa\u002Fb\u002Fc\u002F%7Bfoo%7D\n      eXAMPLE:\u002F\u002Fa\u002F.\u002Fb\u002F..\u002Fb\u002F%63\u002F%7bfoo%7d\n\n   Web user agents, such as browsers, typically apply this type of URI\n   normalization when determining whether a cached response is\n   available.  Syntax-based normalization includes such techniques as\n   case normalization, percent-encoding normalization, and removal of\n   dot-segments.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3936,"children":3938},{"class":3937},"h5",[3939,3945],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3940,"children":3942},{"class":1660,"id":365,"href":3941},"#section-6.2.2.1",[3943],{"type":488,"textContent":3944},"6.2.2.1",{"type":488,"textContent":3946},".  Case Normalization",{"type":488,"textContent":3948},"\n\n   For all URIs, the hexadecimal digits within a percent-encoding\n   triplet (e.g., \"%3a\" versus \"%3A\") are case-insensitive and therefore\n   should be normalized to use uppercase letters for the digits A-F.\n\n   When a URI uses components of the generic syntax, the component\n   syntax equivalence rules always apply; namely, that the scheme and\n   host are case-insensitive and therefore should be normalized to\n   lowercase.  For example, the URI \u003CHTTP:\u002F\u002Fwww.EXAMPLE.com\u002F> is\n   equivalent to \u003Chttp:\u002F\u002Fwww.example.com\u002F>.  The other generic syntax\n   components are assumed to be case-sensitive unless specifically\n   defined otherwise by the scheme (see ",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3950,"children":3951},{"href":1319},[3952],{"type":488,"textContent":3953},"Section 6.2.3",{"type":488,"textContent":2498},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3956,"children":3957},{"class":3937},[3958,3964],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3959,"children":3961},{"class":1660,"id":370,"href":3960},"#section-6.2.2.2",[3962],{"type":488,"textContent":3963},"6.2.2.2",{"type":488,"textContent":3965},".  Percent-Encoding Normalization",{"type":488,"textContent":3967},"\n\n   The percent-encoding mechanism (",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3969,"children":3970},{"href":727},[3971],{"type":488,"textContent":2010},{"type":488,"textContent":3973},") is a frequent source of\n   variance among otherwise identical URIs.  In addition to the case\n   normalization issue noted above, some URI producers percent-encode\n   octets that do not require percent-encoding, resulting in URIs that\n   are equivalent to their non-encoded counterparts.  These URIs should\n   be normalized by decoding any percent-encoded octet that corresponds\n   to an unreserved character, as described in ",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":3975,"children":3976},{"href":755},[3977],{"type":488,"textContent":3978},"Section 2.3",{"type":488,"textContent":3980},".\n\n\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3982,"children":3983},{"class":532},[3984],{"type":488,"textContent":3985},"Berners-Lee, et al.         Standards Track                    [Page 40]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":3988,"children":3989},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":3991,"children":3992},{"class":545},[3993,3997,3998,4006,4007,4018,4020,4024,4026,4031,4033,4038,4039,4048,4050,4055,4057,4062,4064],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3994,"children":3996},{"id":3995},"page-41",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":3999,"children":4000},{"class":532},[4001,4005],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4002,"children":4003},{"href":557},[4004],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":1653},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4008,"children":4009},{"class":3937},[4010,4016],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4011,"children":4013},{"class":1660,"id":375,"href":4012},"#section-6.2.2.3",[4014],{"type":488,"textContent":4015},"6.2.2.3",{"type":488,"textContent":4017},".  Path Segment Normalization",{"type":488,"textContent":4019},"\n\n   The complete path segments \".\" and \"..\" are intended only for use\n   within relative references (",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4021,"children":4022},{"href":941},[4023],{"type":488,"textContent":2771},{"type":488,"textContent":4025},") and are removed as part of\n   the reference resolution process (",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4027,"children":4028},{"href":1094},[4029],{"type":488,"textContent":4030},"Section 5.2",{"type":488,"textContent":4032},").  However, some\n   deployed implementations incorrectly assume that reference resolution\n   is not necessary when the reference is already a URI and thus fail to\n   remove dot-segments when they occur in non-relative paths.  URI\n   normalizers should remove dot-segments by applying the\n   remove_dot_segments algorithm to the path, as described in\n   ",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4034,"children":4035},{"href":1150},[4036],{"type":488,"textContent":4037},"Section 5.2.4",{"type":488,"textContent":2162},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4040,"children":4041},{"class":1864},[4042,4046],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4043,"children":4044},{"class":1660,"id":380,"href":1319},[4045],{"type":488,"textContent":1322},{"type":488,"textContent":4047},".  Scheme-Based Normalization",{"type":488,"textContent":4049},"\n\n   The syntax and semantics of URIs vary from scheme to scheme, as\n   described by the defining specification for each scheme.\n   Implementations may use scheme-specific rules, at further processing\n   cost, to reduce the probability of false negatives.  For example,\n   because the \"http\" scheme makes use of an authority component, has a\n   default port of \"80\", and defines an empty path to be equivalent to\n   \"\u002F\", the following four URIs are equivalent:\n\n      http:\u002F\u002Fexample.com\n      http:\u002F\u002Fexample.com\u002F\n      ",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4051,"children":4053},{"href":4052},"http:\u002F\u002Fexample.com:\u002F",[4054],{"type":488,"textContent":4052},{"type":488,"textContent":4056},"\n      ",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4058,"children":4060},{"href":4059},"http:\u002F\u002Fexample.com:80\u002F",[4061],{"type":488,"textContent":4059},{"type":488,"textContent":4063},"\n\n   In general, a URI that uses the generic syntax for authority with an\n   empty path should be normalized to a path of \"\u002F\".  Likewise, an\n   explicit \":port\", for which the port is empty or the default for the\n   scheme, is equivalent to one where the port and its \":\" delimiter are\n   elided and thus should be removed by scheme-based normalization.  For\n   example, the second URI above is the normal form for the \"http\"\n   scheme.\n\n   Another case where normalization varies by scheme is in the handling\n   of an empty authority component or empty host subcomponent.  For many\n   scheme specifications, an empty authority or host is considered an\n   error; for others, it is considered equivalent to \"localhost\" or the\n   end-user's host.  When a scheme defines a default for authority and a\n   URI reference to that default is desired, the reference should be\n   normalized to an empty authority for the sake of uniformity, brevity,\n   and internationalization.  If, however, either the userinfo or port\n   subcomponents are non-empty, then the host should be given explicitly\n   even if it matches the default.\n\n   Normalization should not remove delimiters when their associated\n   component is empty unless licensed to do so by the scheme\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4065,"children":4066},{"class":532},[4067],{"type":488,"textContent":4068},"Berners-Lee, et al.         Standards Track                    [Page 41]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":4071,"children":4072},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":4074,"children":4075},{"class":545},[4076,4080,4081,4089,4091,4100,4102],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4077,"children":4079},{"id":4078},"page-42",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4082,"children":4083},{"class":532},[4084,4088],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4085,"children":4086},{"href":557},[4087],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":4090},"\n\n\n   specification.  For example, the URI \"http:\u002F\u002Fexample.com\u002F?\" cannot be\n   assumed to be equivalent to any of the examples above.  Likewise, the\n   presence or absence of delimiters within a userinfo subcomponent is\n   usually significant to its interpretation.  The fragment component is\n   not subject to any scheme-based normalization; thus, two URIs that\n   differ only by the suffix \"#\" are considered different regardless of\n   the scheme.\n\n   Some schemes define additional subcomponents that consist of case-\n   insensitive data, giving an implicit license to normalizers to\n   convert this data to a common case (e.g., all lowercase).  For\n   example, URI schemes that define a subcomponent of path to contain an\n   Internet hostname, such as the \"mailto\" URI scheme, cause that\n   subcomponent to be case-insensitive and thus subject to case\n   normalization (e.g., \"mailto:Joe@Example.COM\" is equivalent to\n   \"mailto:Joe@example.com\", even though the generic syntax considers\n   the path component to be case-sensitive).\n\n   Other scheme-specific normalizations are possible.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4092,"children":4093},{"class":1864},[4094,4098],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4095,"children":4096},{"class":1660,"id":385,"href":1334},[4097],{"type":488,"textContent":1337},{"type":488,"textContent":4099},".  Protocol-Based Normalization",{"type":488,"textContent":4101},"\n\n   Substantial effort to reduce the incidence of false negatives is\n   often cost-effective for web spiders.  Therefore, they implement even\n   more aggressive techniques in URI comparison.  For example, if they\n   observe that a URI such as\n\n      http:\u002F\u002Fexample.com\u002Fdata\n\n   redirects to a URI differing only in the trailing slash\n\n      http:\u002F\u002Fexample.com\u002Fdata\u002F\n\n   they will likely regard the two as equivalent in the future.  This\n   kind of technique is only appropriate when equivalence is clearly\n   indicated by both the result of accessing the resources and the\n   common conventions of their scheme's dereference algorithm (in this\n   case, use of redirection by HTTP origin servers to avoid problems\n   with relative references).\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4103,"children":4104},{"class":532},[4105],{"type":488,"textContent":4106},"Berners-Lee, et al.         Standards Track                    [Page 42]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":4109,"children":4110},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":4112,"children":4113},{"class":545},[4114,4118,4119,4127,4128,4137,4139,4148,4150,4159,4161],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4115,"children":4117},{"id":4116},"page-43",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4120,"children":4121},{"class":532},[4122,4126],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4123,"children":4124},{"href":557},[4125],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":1653},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4129,"children":4130},{"class":1656},[4131,4135],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4132,"children":4133},{"class":1660,"id":390,"href":1349},[4134],{"type":488,"textContent":623},{"type":488,"textContent":4136},".  Security Considerations",{"type":488,"textContent":4138},"\n\n   A URI does not in itself pose a security threat.  However, as URIs\n   are often used to provide a compact set of instructions for access to\n   network resources, care must be taken to properly interpret the data\n   within a URI, to prevent that data from causing unintended access,\n   and to avoid including data that should not be revealed in plain\n   text.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4140,"children":4141},{"class":1777},[4142,4146],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4143,"children":4144},{"class":1660,"id":396,"href":1363},[4145],{"type":488,"textContent":1366},{"type":488,"textContent":4147},".  Reliability and Consistency",{"type":488,"textContent":4149},"\n\n   There is no guarantee that once a URI has been used to retrieve\n   information, the same information will be retrievable by that URI in\n   the future.  Nor is there any guarantee that the information\n   retrievable via that URI in the future will be observably similar to\n   that retrieved in the past.  The URI syntax does not constrain how a\n   given scheme or authority apportions its namespace or maintains it\n   over time.  Such guarantees can only be obtained from the person(s)\n   controlling that namespace and the resource in question.  A specific\n   URI scheme may define additional semantics, such as name persistence,\n   if those semantics are required of all naming authorities for that\n   scheme.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4151,"children":4152},{"class":1777},[4153,4157],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4154,"children":4155},{"class":1660,"id":401,"href":1376},[4156],{"type":488,"textContent":1379},{"type":488,"textContent":4158},".  Malicious Construction",{"type":488,"textContent":4160},"\n\n   It is sometimes possible to construct a URI so that an attempt to\n   perform a seemingly harmless, idempotent operation, such as the\n   retrieval of a representation, will in fact cause a possibly damaging\n   remote operation.  The unsafe URI is typically constructed by\n   specifying a port number other than that reserved for the network\n   protocol in question.  The client unwittingly contacts a site running\n   a different protocol service, and data within the URI contains\n   instructions that, when interpreted according to this other protocol,\n   cause an unexpected operation.  A frequent example of such abuse has\n   been the use of a protocol-based scheme with a port component of\n   \"25\", thereby fooling user agent software into sending an unintended\n   or impersonating message via an SMTP server.\n\n   Applications should prevent dereference of a URI that specifies a TCP\n   port number within the \"well-known port\" range (0 - 1023) unless the\n   protocol being used to dereference that URI is compatible with the\n   protocol expected on that well-known port.  Although IANA maintains a\n   registry of well-known ports, applications should make such\n   restrictions user-configurable to avoid preventing the deployment of\n   new services.\n\n\n\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4162,"children":4163},{"class":532},[4164],{"type":488,"textContent":4165},"Berners-Lee, et al.         Standards Track                    [Page 43]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":4168,"children":4169},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":4171,"children":4172},{"class":545},[4173,4177,4178,4186,4188,4197,4199],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4174,"children":4176},{"id":4175},"page-44",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4179,"children":4180},{"class":532},[4181,4185],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4182,"children":4183},{"href":557},[4184],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":4187},"\n\n\n   When a URI contains percent-encoded octets that match the delimiters\n   for a given resolution or dereference protocol (for example, CR and\n   LF characters for the TELNET protocol), these percent-encodings must\n   not be decoded before transmission across that protocol.  Transfer of\n   the percent-encoding, which might violate the protocol, is less\n   harmful than allowing decoded octets to be interpreted as additional\n   operations or parameters, perhaps triggering an unexpected and\n   possibly harmful remote operation.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4189,"children":4190},{"class":1777},[4191,4195],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4192,"children":4193},{"class":1660,"id":406,"href":1389},[4194],{"type":488,"textContent":1392},{"type":488,"textContent":4196},".  Back-End Transcoding",{"type":488,"textContent":4198},"\n\n   When a URI is dereferenced, the data within it is often parsed by\n   both the user agent and one or more servers.  In HTTP, for example, a\n   typical user agent will parse a URI into its five major components,\n   access the authority's server, and send it the data within the\n   authority, path, and query components.  A typical server will take\n   that information, parse the path into segments and the query into\n   key\u002Fvalue pairs, and then invoke implementation-specific handlers to\n   respond to the request.  As a result, a common security concern for\n   server implementations that handle a URI, either as a whole or split\n   into separate components, is proper interpretation of the octet data\n   represented by the characters and percent-encodings within that URI.\n\n   Percent-encoded octets must be decoded at some point during the\n   dereference process.  Applications must split the URI into its\n   components and subcomponents prior to decoding the octets, as\n   otherwise the decoded octets might be mistaken for delimiters.\n   Security checks of the data within a URI should be applied after\n   decoding the octets.  Note, however, that the \"%00\" percent-encoding\n   (NUL) may require special handling and should be rejected if the\n   application is not expecting to receive raw data within a component.\n\n   Special care should be taken when the URI path interpretation process\n   involves the use of a back-end file system or related system\n   functions.  File systems typically assign an operational meaning to\n   special characters, such as the \"\u002F\", \"\\\", \":\", \"[\", and \"]\"\n   characters, and to special device names like \".\", \"..\", \"...\", \"aux\",\n   \"lpt\", etc.  In some cases, merely testing for the existence of such\n   a name will cause the operating system to pause or invoke unrelated\n   system calls, leading to significant security concerns regarding\n   denial of service and unintended data transfer.  It would be\n   impossible for this specification to list all such significant\n   characters and device names.  Implementers should research the\n   reserved names and characters for the types of storage device that\n   may be attached to their applications and restrict the use of data\n   obtained from URI components accordingly.\n\n\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4200,"children":4201},{"class":532},[4202],{"type":488,"textContent":4203},"Berners-Lee, et al.         Standards Track                    [Page 44]",{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":539,"attributes":4206,"children":4207},{"class":541},[],{"type":483,"nodeName":484,"attributes":4209,"children":4210},{"class":545},[4211,4215,4216,4224,4225,4234,4236,4241,4243,4252,4254,4263,4265],{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4212,"children":4214},{"id":4213},"page-45",[],{"type":488,"textContent":537},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4217,"children":4218},{"class":532},[4219,4223],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4220,"children":4221},{"href":557},[4222],{"type":488,"textContent":560},{"type":488,"textContent":562},{"type":488,"textContent":1653},{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4226,"children":4227},{"class":1777},[4228,4232],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4229,"children":4230},{"class":1660,"id":411,"href":1404},[4231],{"type":488,"textContent":1407},{"type":488,"textContent":4233},".  Rare IP Address Formats",{"type":488,"textContent":4235},"\n\n   Although the URI syntax for IPv4address only allows the common\n   dotted-decimal form of IPv4 address literal, many implementations\n   that process URIs make use of platform-dependent system routines,\n   such as gethostbyname() and inet_aton(), to translate the string\n   literal to an actual IP address.  Unfortunately, such system routines\n   often allow and process a much larger set of formats than those\n   described in ",{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4237,"children":4238},{"href":856},[4239],{"type":488,"textContent":4240},"Section 3.2.2",{"type":488,"textContent":4242},".\n\n   For example, many implementations allow dotted forms of three\n   numbers, wherein the last part is interpreted as a 16-bit quantity\n   and placed in the right-most two bytes of the network address (e.g.,\n   a Class B network).  Likewise, a dotted form of two numbers means\n   that the last part is interpreted as a 24-bit quantity and placed in\n   the right-most three bytes of the network address (Class A), and a\n   single number (without dots) is interpreted as a 32-bit quantity and\n   stored directly in the network address.  Adding further to the\n   confusion, some implementations allow each dotted part to be\n   interpreted as decimal, octal, or hexadecimal, as specified in the C\n   language (i.e., a leading 0x or 0X implies hexadecimal; a leading 0\n   implies octal; otherwise, the number is interpreted as decimal).\n\n   These additional IP address formats are not allowed in the URI syntax\n   due to differences between platform implementations.  However, they\n   can become a security concern if an application attempts to filter\n   access to resources based on the IP address in string literal format.\n   If this filtering is performed, literals should be converted to\n   numeric form and filtered based on the numeric value, and not on a\n   prefix or suffix of the string form.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4244,"children":4245},{"class":1777},[4246,4250],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4247,"children":4248},{"class":1660,"id":416,"href":1419},[4249],{"type":488,"textContent":1422},{"type":488,"textContent":4251},".  Sensitive Information",{"type":488,"textContent":4253},"\n\n   URI producers should not provide a URI that contains a username or\n   password that is intended to be secret.  URIs are frequently\n   displayed by browsers, stored in clear text bookmarks, and logged by\n   user agent history and intermediary applications (proxies).  A\n   password appearing within the userinfo component is deprecated and\n   should be considered an error (or simply ignored) except in those\n   rare cases where the 'password' parameter is intended to be public.\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4255,"children":4256},{"class":1777},[4257,4261],{"type":483,"nodeName":491,"attributes":4258,"children":4259},{"class":1660,"id":421,"href":1432},[4260],{"type":488,"textContent":1435},{"type":488,"textContent":4262},".  Semantic Attacks",{"type":488,"textContent":4264},"\n\n   Because the userinfo subcomponent is rarely used and appears before\n   the host in the authority component, it can be used to construct a\n   URI intended to mislead a human user by appearing to identify one\n   (trusted) naming authority while actually identifying a different\n   authority hidden behind the noise.  For example\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4266,"children":4267},{"class":532},[4268],{"type":488,"textContent":4269},"Berners-Lee, et al. Delimiting a URI in Context",{"type":488,"textContent":4960},"\n\n   URIs are often transmitted through formats that do not provide a\n   clear context for their interpretation.  For example, there are many\n   occasions when a URI is included in plain text; examples include text\n   sent in email, USENET news, and on printed paper.  In such cases, it\n   is important to be able to delimit the URI from the rest of the text,\n   and in particular from punctuation marks that might be mistaken for\n   part of the URI.\n\n   In practice, URIs are delimited in a variety of ways, but usually\n   within double-quotes \"http:\u002F\u002Fexample.com\u002F\", angle brackets\n   \u003Chttp:\u002F\u002Fexample.com\u002F>, or just by using whitespace:\n\n\n\n",{"type":483,"nodeName":523,"attributes":4962,"children":4963},{"class":532},[4964],{"type":488,"textContent":4965},"Berners-Lee, et al.
